title: Splitting one long test, and the problem it creates

parts.title: Splitting one long test, and the problem it creates

blocks.text:
# Week 2 - Day 5 - Fundamentals - Splitting one long test, and the problem it creates

By the end of this lesson you will have run one long test, split it into five small
ones, and watched a real failure appear that has nothing to do with a typo — it's
Playwright's central design decision showing up for the first time.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Goals** | Watch a correct test fail because of a design decision, not a bug. |
| **Prerequisites** | [test() and the assertions gap](/learn/w1/d5/p2) · [the page fixture](/learn/w1/d5/p1) |
| **Environment** | test-runner — the studio editor runs library code, so follow these in your own checkout |
| **Scope** | [Implementation](/learn/w2/d5/p3) shows the fix's shape; week 3 builds it properly |

> **Follow this one in your own project.** These examples are run by the Playwright test runner, which the editor here does not provide. Copy them into your own checkout to run them.

## One test, five things

A test that logs in, views transaction history, pays a bill, checks billing history, and
logs out reads fine — until it fails. When it does, the failure just says "this test
failed"; you're left guessing which of the five steps broke.

There's also a harder ceiling: **every Playwright test has a default budget of 30
seconds.** Each extra real step — a navigation, a slow render — eats into that budget,
and a test doing five things is five times more likely to bump into it than a test doing
one.

## Example 1 — the one long test, run for real

**Objective:** see the actual duration of a single test doing five real things.

> ▶ **Run it yourself too:** `npx playwright test week2/generated/day5-one-long-test.spec.ts`

**Expected result:** `1 passed`, in roughly 25–30 seconds — measured against the live
banking app while writing this lesson. That's already within a few seconds of the
default 30-second test timeout, for a journey that does nothing unusual.

Playwright's own reporter has a name for this: a **slow test file** warning appears when
a file's tests take a long time in total, suggesting you split them so they can run in
parallel. You've just watched a smaller version of that same pressure build inside a
single test.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same experiment, a shorter journey: in your own checkout, write the same style of single test doing only three of the banking app's steps instead of five, and compare the duration the reporter prints against the five-step run. You are measuring how much of the 30-second budget one real step costs — which is the number that decides when a test is too long.

blocks.text:
## Example 2 — split it, the obvious way

**Objective:** break the journey into small `test()`s — one per concern, the same
response to "each failure should name one thing" that [Day 1](/learn/w1/d5/p2)
already taught you to want from an assertion.

> ▶ **Run it yourself too:** `npx playwright test week2/generated/day5-split-isolation.spec.ts`

**Expected result (verified live, reproduced twice while writing this):** `1 failed, 1
passed`.

```
Error: expect(locator).toBeVisible() failed
Locator: getByText('Leela')
Expected: visible
Error: element(s) not found
```

Read `test 2` again — there's no bug in it. It goes to `/dashboard` and looks for the
name. The name just isn't there, because **`test 2` never logged in.** `test 1` did, but
that session didn't carry over.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same failure, a different pair: split some other two-step journey so the second test needs something only the first one set up, and read the error it gives you. Note what the message actually says — it names an element that was not found, never a session that was not there. The error describes the symptom; the cause is yours to know.

blocks.text:
## Why: every test gets a fresh `page`

This isn't a quirk of this app — it's Playwright's central design decision. Each `test()`
receives its own `page`: a blank tab, no cookies, no storage, nothing carried over from
any other test. That's what makes tests safe to run in any order, in parallel, and
without one test's failure corrupting the next one's starting state.

The cost is the flip side of the benefit: state you *want* to keep — like being logged
in — has to be shared on purpose. Splitting a test for readability is exactly the moment
this becomes visible, because now you have two tests where you used to have a single
continuous story.

**What's next fixes this for real.** [Implementation](/learn/w2/d5/p3) previews the shape of the
fix; [Week 3 - Day 2 - TypeScript](/learn/w3/d2/p1) and
[Week 3 - Day 2 - Fundamentals](/learn/w3/d2/p2) build it properly, with hooks named and
explained.

## Best practices

- Split a long test by concern — the readability win is real.
- Before you split, ask what state the later pieces need that only the earlier ones set
  up. Login is the most common one.
- Don't "fix" this by copy-pasting the login steps into every test — [Implementation](/learn/w2/d5/p3)
  shows why sharing beats repeating once you have more than two or three tests.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Splitting a long test without checking what state carries over | one or more of the new tests fail immediately | identify the shared setup, then read [Implementation](/learn/w2/d5/p3) |
| Assuming `toHaveURL(/dashboard/)` proves you're logged in | it doesn't — this app has no route guard, so a logged-out page still loads at that URL | assert on user-specific content instead (the name, an account number) |
| Re-running the whole login in every split test "just in case" | works, but every test pays the login cost again | fine for a couple of tests; [Implementation](/learn/w2/d5/p3) previews the alternative once it doesn't scale |
After the split, `test 2` fails with `element(s) not found` on `getByText('Leela')`. What is wrong with `test 2`?

options: Its locator is wrong — the name is rendered differently on that route
Nothing. It never logged in, because `test 1`'s session did not carry over to it
It ran before `test 1` finished, so the dashboard had not loaded yet
checkpoint.explanation: There is no bug in `test 2`. It navigates to `/dashboard` and looks for the name, and the name genuinely is not there — every `test()` receives its own `page`: a blank tab, no cookies, no storage. That isolation is what makes tests safe to run in any order and in parallel; the cost is that state you *want* has to be shared deliberately.

blocks.text: The failure message names a missing element. Why is that worth noticing?

options: Because it means the locator needs replacing before anything else
Because the error reports the symptom, not the cause — nothing in it mentions a missing session
Because Playwright suppresses the real error when tests run in a describe block
checkpoint.explanation: An isolation problem always surfaces as something further downstream — an element that is not there, a value that is empty. The runner cannot know you *expected* to still be signed in. Recognizing the shape of this failure is most of what today is for.

blocks.text: Why is `await expect(page).toHaveURL(/dashboard/)` not proof that you are logged in?

options: Because `toHaveURL` does not retry, so it can pass before the redirect
Because this app has no route guard — a logged-out page still loads at that URL
Because the URL is set before the session is created
checkpoint.explanation: Nothing stops an unauthenticated browser loading `/dashboard` here; it just renders without the user's data. Assert on something only a signed-in user could see, such as the name or an account number. That is the same "assert something observable" habit from [Day 2 - Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d2/p2).

blocks.text:
- **Every `test()` gets its own fresh `page`** — a blank tab, no cookies, nothing carried over. That is Playwright's central design decision, not a quirk of this app.
- The benefit is order-independence and parallelism. The cost is that shared state has to be shared on purpose.
- Splitting a long test is the moment you first pay that cost, because a continuous story becomes several independent ones.
- An isolation failure never announces itself — it shows up as a missing element somewhere downstream.
- Assert on user-specific content, not on a URL, to prove you are signed in.
- Copy-pasting login into every test works, and stops working once there are more than two or three.

## What's next

[Implementation](/learn/w2/d5/p3) previews the fix — not the full lesson, that's week3's job.

parts.title: Preview: the shape of the fix

blocks.text:
# Week 2 - Day 5 - Implementation - Preview: the shape of the fix

**This lesson does not teach hooks.** It shows the fix from [Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d5/p2) running for real,
names the pieces, and points you at where each one is actually explained.

> **Follow this one in your own project.** These examples are run by the Playwright test runner, which the editor here does not provide. Copy them into your own checkout to run them.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | a preview: the fix shown running for real, with its pieces named |
| **Scope** | This lesson shows the problem that hooks solve. Hooks themselves are taught in [Week 3 - Day 2 - TypeScript](/learn/w3/d2/p1) and [Week 3 - Day 2 - Fundamentals](/learn/w3/d2/p2), because the tool deserves a full lesson. |

## The shape, named but not explained

| Piece | What it's for |
|---|---|
| `browser.newContext()` | a fresh, isolated environment you create yourself — instead of one being created per test automatically |
| `test.beforeAll(...)` | runs once, before the first test in a group — where you'd create that shared context and log in |
| `test.afterAll(...)` | runs once, after the last test — where you'd close it |
| `test.describe(...)` | groups the tests that share that context |
| `test.describe.configure({ mode: "serial" })` | tells Playwright these tests depend on each other and must not run at the same time |

All five names come from [Week 3 - Day 2 - TypeScript](/learn/w3/d2/p1) (the TypeScript
underneath them — arrow functions passed as hook bodies) and
[Week 3 - Day 2 - Fundamentals](/learn/w3/d2/p2) (what each one actually does, and why). This
lesson only proves the shape works.

## Watching it work

**Objective:** the exact two tests from [Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d5/p2) — Example 2 — passing this time, because
they share one login instead of each getting a blank page.

> ▶ **Run it yourself too:** `npx playwright test week2/generated/day5-shared-context-preview.spec.ts`

**Expected result:** `2 passed` — verified live while writing this lesson.

One measured detail worth keeping, even at preview depth: `test 2` doesn't call
`page.goto()` again. This app keeps its session **in memory only** (no cookies, no
`localStorage`) — a full navigation reloads the page and wipes it, whether or not the
context is shared. Sharing the context gets you the same tab still sitting where test 1
left it; it doesn't survive a fresh `goto()` any more than an isolated one would.
Of the five pieces named here, which one runs once before the first test in the group — the place a shared login would go?

checkpoint.explanation: `test.beforeAll` runs once before the group, and `test.afterAll` once after it — which is where the context gets created and closed. `test.describe` only groups; `mode: "serial"` only says the tests depend on each other; `browser.newContext()` is the thing being created. Week 3 is where each of these stops being a name and starts being a tool.

blocks.text: In the preview spec, `test 2` deliberately does not call `page.goto()`. Why not?

options: Because a shared context forbids navigation once a test has started
Because this app keeps its session in memory only, so a full navigation reloads the page and wipes it — shared context or not
Because `goto()` would create a second page inside the same context
checkpoint.explanation: No cookies, no `localStorage` — the session lives in memory. Sharing the context hands `test 2` the same tab still sitting where `test 1` left it; it does not make a fresh `goto()` survivable. A measured detail worth keeping, because it is the kind of thing that makes a "correct" fix look broken.

blocks.text:
- The fix is a context you create and share deliberately, rather than the per-test one Playwright makes for you.
- `beforeAll` / `afterAll` open and close it; `describe` groups the tests; `serial` mode says they depend on each other.
- Sharing a context shares the tab and its in-memory state — it is not a way to make navigation preserve a session.
- This is the shape only. Week 3 opens by building it for real.

## What's next

[Week 3 - Day 2 - TypeScript](/learn/w3/d2/p1) and [Week 3 - Day 2 - Fundamentals](/learn/w3/d2/p2)
build this properly: why `page` and `browser` have different scope, all four hooks
explained, `test.describe` grouping, and when to reach for `mode: "serial"`. This preview
stops here on purpose — that's next week's first lesson, not this lesson's.

blocks.text:
# Week 2 - Day 5 - Practice - Splitting tests, and the isolation problem

Three problems. The third one has no code to write — it's a question, because the real
hook lesson is week3's job, not this lesson's.

Start in a fresh cell in this lesson. When a problem asks for a spec file, write it
into `week2/generated/` and run it with `npx playwright test`.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | reproduce the failure, then fix it, then answer a question |
| **Environment** | Problem 3 is a written reflection. Hooks are taught in Week 3. |
| **Scope** | These problems close Week 2, which covered locators, assertions, unique data, the sibling axis, and test isolation. |

## End of week 2

Locators (role, placeholder, XPath, CSS, the sibling axis), real assertions, unique test
data, and the isolation problem a split test creates are all in hand now. week3 starts
immediately with the fix — hooks — and then configuration.

problems.statement:
**What to build.** Pick a different two-step scenario on the banking app (for example:
test 1 navigates to Pay Bills and reads a value; test 2 tries to read something from
Billing History that assumes test 1 already put you there) and reproduce the isolation
failure yourself — two `test()`s in one `describe`, the second assuming state from the
first.

**Where.** A spec in `week2/generated/`.

**How you will know it worked.** The second test fails with a real Playwright error, not
a typo of yours — and you can explain in one sentence why it's failing.

> **Hint** — [Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d5/p2), Example 2 is the template. Change *what* state test 2 assumes, not
> the shape.

**What to build.** Fix the spec you just wrote using `browser.newContext()` — the same
shape from [Implementation](/learn/w2/d5/p3) — and confirm both tests now pass.

**Where.** The same spec file, or a new one in `week2/generated/`.

**How you will know it worked.** `2 passed`, where a moment ago it was `1 failed, 1
passed`.

[Implementation](/learn/w2/d5/p3) named five pieces: `browser.newContext()`, `test.beforeAll`, `test.afterAll`,
`test.describe`, and `mode: "serial"`.

**Question:** if you wanted that shared context built exactly **once** for every test in
a whole spec file — not re-created per test — which single hook name from that list is
the one doing that job, and why does it have to be the one that runs *before the first
test*, rather than one that runs before *each* test?

Write your answer as a comment in a cell below. There's no code to run here — check
your reasoning against [Week 3 - Day 2 - Fundamentals](/learn/w3/d2/p2) once you get there.
problems.stub: // Problem 3 — your reasoning here, as a comment. No code to run.
problems.solution:
**The answer: `test.beforeAll`.**

> `test.beforeAll` runs **once per file**, before any test in it. So a context created inside it is built exactly once and every test in the file shares it. `test.beforeEach` would run before *each* test and rebuild the context every time — which is the per-test isolation Playwright already provides by default, at the cost of a login on every test.

**Where the other four sit:**

| Piece | What it does |
|---|---|
| `browser.newContext()` | Creates the shared session. It is *what* is shared. |
| **`test.beforeAll`** | Runs it **once**. It is *why* it is shared rather than rebuilt. |
| `test.afterAll` | Closes it once, at the end. Without this the context leaks. |
| `test.describe` | Groups the tests so "once per file" has a scope, and gives the block a name in the report. |
| `mode: "serial"` | Stops them running in parallel and fighting over the one page. |

**The distinction worth holding on to.** `beforeAll` is about *how often setup runs*; `mode: "serial"` is about *whether tests may overlap*. They are easy to conflate because a shared context needs both, but they answer different questions — and in Week 3, when you meet hooks properly, you will use each of them without the other.

> `afterAll` is the one people leave out. It costs nothing on a two-test file and quietly exhausts a CI runner on a large suite.
